runs\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Tracing\\\\n\\\\nThe Agents SDK includes built-in tracing, collecting a comprehensive record of events during an agent run: LLM generations, tool calls, handoffs, guardrails, and even custom events that occur. Using the [Traces dashboard](https://platform.openai.com/traces), you can debug, visualize, and monitor your workflows during development and in production.\\\\n\\\\nNote\\\\n\\\\nTracing is enabled by default in server runtimes (Node.js, Deno, Bun). It is disabled by default in browsers and when `NODE_ENV=test`.\\\\n\\\\nThere are two ways to disable tracing in server environments:\\\\n\\\\n1.   You can globally disable tracing by setting the env var `OPENAI_AGENTS_DISABLE_TRACING=1`\\\\n2.   You can disable tracing on a runner by setting [`RunConfig.tracingDisabled`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/type-aliases/runconfig/#tracingdisabled) to `true` in `new Runner(...)`\\\\n\\\\n**_For organizations operating under a Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy using OpenAI’s APIs, tracing is unavailable._**\\\\n\\\\n## Export loop lifecycle\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Export loop lifecycle”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#export-loop-lifecycle)\\\\n\\\\nIn supported server runtimes, traces are exported on a regular interval. In some runtimes, including Cloudflare Workers, the automatic export loop is unavailable even though tracing itself is still enabled. In those environments you should call `getGlobalTraceProvider().forceFlush()` as part of your request lifecycle to export queued traces before the runtime is torn down.\\\\n\\\\nThis guidance does not apply to browsers because tracing is disabled there by default.\\\\n\\\\nFor example, in a Cloudflare Worker, you should wrap your code into a `try/catch/finally` block and use `forceFlush()` with `waitUntil` to ensure that traces are exported before the worker exits.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { getGlobalTraceProvider } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nexport default {  async fetch(request, env, ctx): Promise<Response> {    try {      // your agent code here      return new Response(`success`);    } catch (error) {      console.error(error);      return new Response(String(error), { status: 500 });    } finally {      // make sure to flush any remaining traces before exiting      ctx.waitUntil(getGlobalTraceProvider().forceFlush());    }  },};\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Traces and spans\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Traces and spans”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#traces-and-spans)\\\\n\\\\n*   **Traces** represent a single end-to-end operation of a “workflow”. They’re composed of Spans. Traces have the following properties: \\\\n    *   `workflow_name`: This is the logical workflow or app. For example “Code generation” or “Customer service”.\\\\n    *   `trace_id`: A unique ID for the trace. Automatically generated if you don’t pass one. Must have the format `trace_<32_alphanumeric>`.\\\\n    *   `group_id`: Optional group ID, to link multiple traces from the same conversation. For example, you might use a chat thread ID.\\\\n    *   `disabled`: If True, the trace will not be recorded.\\\\n    *   `metadata`: Optional metadata for the trace.\\\\n\\\\n*   **Spans** represent operations that have a start and end time. Spans have: \\\\n    *   `started_at` and `ended_at` timestamps.\\\\n    *   `trace_id`, to represent the trace they belong to\\\\n    *   `parent_id`, which points to the parent Span of this Span (if any)\\\\n    *   `span_data`, which is information about the Span. For example, `AgentSpanData` contains information about the Agent, `GenerationSpanData` contains information about the LLM generation, etc.\\\\n\\\\n## Default tracing\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Default tracing”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#default-tracing)\\\\n\\\\nBy default, the SDK traces the following:\\\\n\\\\n*   The entire `run()` or `Runner.run()` is wrapped in a `Trace`.\\\\n*   Each top-level runner invocation is wrapped in a `TaskSpan`.\\\\n*   Each time an agent runs, it is wrapped in an `AgentSpan`.\\\\n*   Each agent loop iteration is wrapped in a `TurnSpan`.\\\\n*   LLM generations are wrapped in a `GenerationSpan`.\\\\n*   Function tool calls are each wrapped in a `FunctionSpan`.\\\\n*   Guardrails are wrapped in a `GuardrailSpan`.\\\\n*   Handoffs are wrapped in a `HandoffSpan`.\\\\n\\\\nThe default hierarchy is `TaskSpan` → `AgentSpan` → `TurnSpan`, with model and tool work nested under the turn. A task span aggregates request and token usage for the invocation. Each turn span records the turn number, agent name, and input, output, cached-input, and cache-write token counts.\\\\n\\\\nTask and turn spans are enabled by default. Set `tracing: { includeTaskAndTurnSpans: false }` on a `Runner` or an individual run to omit this additional hierarchy. Per-run tracing options override the runner-level setting.\\\\n\\\\nBy default, the trace is named “Agent workflow”. You can set this name if you use `withTrace`, or you can configure the name and other properties with the [`RunConfig.workflowName`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/type-aliases/runconfig/#workflowname).\\\\n\\\\nIn addition, you can set up [custom trace processors](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#custom-tracing-processors) to push traces to other destinations (as a replacement, or secondary destination).\\\\n\\\\n### Realtime agent tracing\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Realtime agent tracing”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#realtime-agent-tracing)\\\\n\\\\nIf you are using `RealtimeAgent` and `RealtimeSession` with the default OpenAI Realtime API, tracing will automatically happen on the Realtime API side unless you disable it on the `RealtimeSession` using `tracingDisabled: true` or using the `OPENAI_AGENTS_DISABLE_TRACING` environment variable.\\\\n\\\\nCheck out the [Realtime agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/voice-agents) for more details.\\\\n\\\\n## Higher level traces\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Higher level traces”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#higher-level-traces)\\\\n\\\\nSometimes, you might want multiple calls to `run()` to be part of a single trace. You can do this by wrapping the entire code in a `withTrace()`.\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run, withTrace } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Joke generator',  instructions: 'Tell funny jokes.',});\\\\nawait withTrace('Joke workflow', async () => {  const result = await run(agent, 'Tell me a joke');  const secondResult = await run(    agent,    `Rate this joke: ${result.finalOutput}`,  );  console.log(`Joke: ${result.finalOutput}`);  console.log(`Rating: ${secondResult.finalOutput}`);});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n1.   Because the two calls to `run` are wrapped in a `withTrace()`, the individual runs will be part of the overall trace rather than creating two traces.\\\\n\\\\n## Creating traces\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Creating traces”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#creating-traces)\\\\n\\\\nYou can use the [`withTrace()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/functions/withtrace/) function to create a trace. Alternatively, you can use `getGlobalTraceProvider().createTrace()` to create a new trace manually and pass it into `withTrace()`.\\\\n\\\\nThe current trace is tracked via a [Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage`](https://nodejs.org/api/async_context.html#class-asynclocalstorage) or the respective environment polyfills. This means that it works with concurrency automatically.\\\\n\\\\n## Creating spans\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Creating spans”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#creating-spans)\\\\n\\\\nYou can use the various `create*Span()` methods, such as `createTaskSpan()`, `createTurnSpan()`, `createGenerationSpan()`, and `createFunctionSpan()`, to create a span. Matching helpers such as `withTaskSpan()` and `withTurnSpan()` create and manage the span lifecycle around a callback. In general, you don’t need to manually create spans. A [`createCustomSpan()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/functions/createcustomspan/) function is available for tracking custom span information.\\\\n\\\\nSpans are automatically part of the current trace, and are nested under the nearest current span, which is tracked via a [Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage`](https://nodejs.org/api/async_context.html#class-asynclocalstorage) or the respective environment polyfills.\\\\n\\\\n## Sensitive data\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Sensitive data”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#sensitive-data)\\\\n\\\\nCertain spans may capture potentially sensitive data.\\\\n\\\\nThe `createGenerationSpan()` stores the inputs/outputs of the LLM generation, and `createFunctionSpan()` stores the inputs/outputs of function calls. These may contain sensitive data, so you can disable capturing that data via [`RunConfig.traceIncludeSensitiveData`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/type-aliases/runconfig/#traceincludesensitivedata).\\\\n\\\\n## OpenAI tracing exporter\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “OpenAI tracing exporter”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#openai-tracing-exporter)\\\\n\\\\nIn supported server runtimes, the default tracing setup already exports to OpenAI. Use `setTracingExportApiKey()` when trace export should use a different credential than `OPENAI_API_KEY`.\\\\n\\\\nIf you need custom ingest behavior, instantiate [`OpenAITracingExporter`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-openai/classes/openaitracingexporter) yourself and install it with `setTraceProcessors(...)` or `addTraceProcessor(...)`. The exporter supports `apiKey`, `endpoint`, `organization`, `project`, `maxRetries`, `baseDelay`, and `maxDelay`.\\\\n\\\\nIf you replace the default processors and later want to restore the default OpenAI exporter with a batch processor, call [`setDefaultOpenAITracingExporter()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-openai/functions/setdefaultopenaitracingexporter/).\\\\n\\\\n## Custom tracing processors\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Custom tracing processors”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#custom-tracing-processors)\\\\n\\\\nThe high level architecture for tracing is:\\\\n\\\\n*   At initialization, we create a global [`TraceProvider`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/classes/traceprovider), which is responsible for creating traces and can be accessed through [`getGlobalTraceProvider()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/functions/getglobaltraceprovider/).\\\\n*   We configure the `TraceProvider` with a [`BatchTraceProcessor`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/classes/batchtraceprocessor/) that sends traces/spans in batches to a [`OpenAITracingExporter`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-openai/classes/openaitracingexporter/), which exports the spans and traces to the OpenAI backend in batches.\\\\n\\\\nTo customize this default setup, to send traces to alternative or additional backends or modifying exporter behavior, you have two options:\\\\n\\\\n1.   [`addTraceProcessor()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/functions/addtraceprocessor) lets you add an **additional** trace processor that will receive traces and spans as they are ready. This lets you do your own processing in addition to sending traces to OpenAI’s backend.\\\\n2.   [`setTraceProcessors()`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/functions/settraceprocessors) lets you **replace** the default processors with your own trace processors. This means traces will not be sent to the OpenAI backend unless you include a `TracingProcessor` that does so.\\\\n\\\\n## External tracing processors list\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “External tracing processors list”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tracing#external-tracing-processors-list)\\\\n\\\\n*   [AgentOps](https://docs.agentops.ai/v2/usage/typescript-sdk#openai-agents-integration)\\\\n*   [Respan](https://www.respan.ai/docs/integrations/openai-agents-sdk)\\\\n*   [PromptLayer](https://docs.promptlayer.com/languages/integrations#openai-agents-sdk)\\\\n*   [Latitude](https://docs.latitude.so/telemetry/frameworks/openai-agents)\\\\n*   [Traccia](https://traccia.ai/docs/integrations/openai-agents)\\\",\\\"publishedTime\\\":\\\"Wed, 19 Aug 2026 15:08:58 GMT\\\",\\\"links\\\":{\\\"Traces scratch\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Quickstart\\\\n\\\\nLooking for sandbox agents?\\\\n\\\\nThis quickstart builds a text agent that runs in your app process. If you want an agent with an isolated filesystem workspace, shell commands, and sandbox session state, start with the [Sandbox agents quickstart](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sandbox-agents).\\\\n\\\\n## Project Setup\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Project Setup”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#project-setup)\\\\n\\\\n1.   Create a project and initialize npm. You’ll only need to do this once.\\\\n\\\\nTerminal window\\\\n\\\\n`mkdir my_projectcd my_projectnpm init -y`    \\\\n2.   Install the Agents SDK and Zod. The SDK uses Zod v4 for tool schemas and structured outputs.\\\\n\\\\nTerminal window\\\\n\\\\n`npm install @openai/agents zod`    \\\\n3.   Set an OpenAI API key. If you don’t have one, follow [these instructions](https://platform.openai.com/docs/quickstart#create-and-export-an-api-key) to create an OpenAI API key.\\\\n\\\\nTerminal window\\\\n\\\\n`export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...`    \\\\nAlternatively you can call `setDefaultOpenAIKey('<api key>')` to set the key programmatically and use `setTracingExportApiKey('<api key>')` for tracing. See [the config guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/config) for more details.\\\\n\\\\n## Create your first agent\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Create your first agent”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#create-your-first-agent)\\\\n\\\\nAgents are defined with instructions and a name.\\\\n\\\\nCreate an agent\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Run your first agent\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Run your first agent”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#run-your-first-agent)\\\\n\\\\nYou can use the `run` method to run your agent. You trigger a run by passing both the agent you want to start on and the input you want to pass in.\\\\n\\\\nThis will return a result that contains the final output and any actions that were performed during that run.\\\\n\\\\nRun an agent\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\nconst result = await run(agent, 'When did sharks first appear?');\\\\nconsole.log(result.finalOutput);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor a second turn, you can either pass `result.history` back into `run()`, attach a [session](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions), or reuse OpenAI server-managed state with `conversationId` / `previousResponseId`. The [running agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents) guide compares these approaches.\\\\n\\\\n## Give your agent tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Give your agent tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#give-your-agent-tools)\\\\n\\\\nYou can give an agent tools to use to look up information or perform actions.\\\\n\\\\nAdd a tool\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, tool } from '@openai/agents';import { z } from 'zod';\\\\nconst historyFunFact = tool({  // The name of the tool will be used by the agent to tell what tool to use.  name: 'history_fun_fact',  // The description is used to describe when to use the tool by telling it what it does.  description: 'Give a fun fact about a historical event',  // This tool takes no parameters, so we provide an empty Zod object.  parameters: z.object({}),  execute: async () => {    // The output will be returned back to the agent to use.    return 'Sharks are older than trees.';  },});\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',  // Add the tool to the agent.  tools: [historyFunFact],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Add a few more agents\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Add a few more agents”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#add-a-few-more-agents)\\\\n\\\\nDefine additional specialist agents to break down problems into smaller parts, keep each specialist focused on one task, and use different models for different problems.\\\\n\\\\nCreate specialist agents\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst historyTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. The [running agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents) guide compares these approaches.\\\\n\\\\n## Give your agent tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Give your agent tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#give-your-agent-tools)\\\\n\\\\nYou can give an agent tools to use to look up information or perform actions.\\\\n\\\\nAdd a tool\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, tool } from '@openai/agents';import { z } from 'zod';\\\\nconst historyFunFact = tool({  // The name of the tool will be used by the agent to tell what tool to use.  name: 'history_fun_fact',  // The description is used to describe when to use the tool by telling it what it does.  description: 'Give a fun fact about a historical event',  // This tool takes no parameters, so we provide an empty Zod object.  parameters: z.object({}),  execute: async () => {    // The output will be returned back to the agent to use.    return 'Sharks are older than trees.';  },});\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',  // Add the tool to the agent.  tools: [historyFunFact],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Add a few more agents\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Add a few more agents”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#add-a-few-more-agents)\\\\n\\\\nDefine additional specialist agents to break down problems into smaller parts, keep each specialist focused on one task, and use different models for different problems.\\\\n\\\\nCreate specialist agents\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst historyTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\nconst mathTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Math Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide help with math problems. Explain your reasoning at each step and include examples',});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Define your handoffs\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Define your handoffs”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#define-your-handoffs)\\\\n\\\\nTo orchestrate multiple agents, define an agent’s `handoffs`. When a handoff is selected during a run, the runner automatically transfers the conversation to the target agent.\\\\n\\\\nDefine handoffs\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst historyTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\nconst mathTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Math Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide help with math problems. Explain your reasoning at each step and include examples',});\\\\n// Use Agent.create() to keep handoff output types aligned.const triageAgent = Agent.create({  name: 'Triage Agent',  instructions:    \\\\\\\"You determine which agent to use based on the user's homework question\\\\\\\",  handoffs: [historyTutorAgent, mathTutorAgent],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAfter your run you can see which agent generated the final response by looking at the `lastAgent` property on the result.\\\\n\\\\n## Run the agent orchestration\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Run the agent orchestration”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#run-the-agent-orchestration)\\\\n\\\\nThe runner handles executing individual agents, any handoffs, and any tool calls.\\\\n\\\\nRun agent orchestration\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst historyTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\nconst mathTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Math Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide help with math problems. Explain your reasoning at each step and include examples',});\\\\nconst triageAgent = Agent.create({  name: 'Triage Agent',  instructions:    \\\\\\\"You determine which agent to use based on the user's homework question\\\\\\\",  handoffs: [historyTutorAgent, mathTutorAgent],});\\\\nasync function main() {  const result = await run(triageAgent, 'What is the capital of France?');  console.log(result.finalOutput);}\\\\nmain().catch((err) => console.error(err));\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## Putting it all together\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Putting it all together”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#putting-it-all-together)\\\\n\\\\nLet’s put it all together into one full example. Place this into your `index.js` file and run it. If your app is already set up for TypeScript, you can use `index.ts` instead.\\\\n\\\\nQuickstart\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst historyTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'History Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide assistance with historical queries. Explain important events and context clearly.',});\\\\nconst mathTutorAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Math Tutor',  instructions:    'You provide help with math problems. Explain your reasoning at each step and include examples',});\\\\nconst triageAgent = Agent.create({  name: 'Triage Agent',  instructions:    \\\\\\\"You determine which agent to use based on the user's homework question\\\\\\\",  handoffs: [historyTutorAgent, mathTutorAgent],});\\\\nasync function main() {  const result = await run(triageAgent, 'What is the capital of France?');  console.log(result.finalOutput);}\\\\nmain().catch((err) => console.error(err));\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n## View your traces\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “View your traces”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#view-your-traces)\\\\n\\\\nThe Agents SDK automatically generates traces. You can use these traces to review how your agents are operating, what tools they called, and which agents received handoffs.\\\\n\\\\nTo review what happened during your agent run, navigate to the [Trace viewer in the OpenAI Dashboard](https://platform.openai.com/traces).\\\\n\\\\n## Next steps\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Next tools\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Tools\\\\n\\\\nTools let an Agent **take actions** – fetch data, call external APIs, execute code, or even use a computer. The JavaScript/TypeScript SDK supports seven categories:\\\\n\\\\n> Read this page after [Agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents) once you know which agent should own the task and you want to give it capabilities. If you are still deciding between delegation patterns, see [Agent orchestration](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent).\\\\n\\\\n1.   **Hosted OpenAI tools** – run alongside the model on OpenAI servers. _(web search, file search, code interpreter, image generation, tool search)_\\\\n2.   **Built-in execution tools** – SDK-provided tools that execute outside the model. _(computer use and apply\\\\\\\\_patch run locally; shell can run locally or in hosted containers)_\\\\n3.   **Function tools** – wrap any local function with a JSON schema so the LLM can call it.\\\\n4.   **Agents as tools** – expose an entire Agent as a callable tool.\\\\n5.   **MCP servers** – attach a Model Context Protocol server (local or remote).\\\\n6.   **Sandbox capabilities** – attach workspace-scoped shell, filesystem, skills, memory, or compaction tools to a `SandboxAgent`.\\\\n7.   **Experimental: Codex tool** – wrap the Codex SDK as a function tool to run workspace-aware tasks.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Tool categories\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Tool categories”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#tool-categories)\\\\n\\\\nThe rest of this guide first covers each tool category, then summarizes cross-cutting tool selection and prompting guidance.\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Hosted tools (OpenAI Responses API)\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “1. Hosted tools (OpenAI Responses API)”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#1-hosted-tools-openai-responses-api)\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use the `OpenAIResponsesModel` you can add the following built‑in tools:\\\\n\\\\n| Tool | Type string | Purpose |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| Web search | `'web_search'` | Internet search. |\\\\n| File / retrieval search | `'file_search'` | Query vector stores hosted on OpenAI. |\\\\n| Code Interpreter | `'code_interpreter'` | Run code in a sandboxed environment. |\\\\n| Image generation | `'image_generation'` | Generate images based on text. |\\\\n| Tool search | `'tool_search'` | Load deferred function tools, namespaces, or searchable MCP tools at runtime. |\\\\n| Programmatic Tool Calling | `'programmatic_tool_calling'` | Run model-generated JavaScript that coordinates eligible tools. |\\\\n\\\\nHosted tools\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  codeInterpreterTool,  fileSearchTool,  imageGenerationTool,  webSearchTool,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Travel assistant',  tools: [    webSearchTool({ searchContextSize: 'medium' }),    fileSearchTool('VS_ID', { maxNumResults: 3 }),    codeInterpreterTool(),    imageGenerationTool({ size: '1024x1024' }),  ],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe SDK provides helper functions that return hosted tool definitions:\\\\n\\\\n| Helper function | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- |\\\\n| `webSearchTool(options?)` | JS-friendly options such as `searchContextSize`, `userLocation`, and `filters.allowedDomains`. |\\\\n| `fileSearchTool(ids, options?)` | Accepts one or more vector store IDs as the first argument, plus options like `maxNumResults`, `includeSearchResults`, `rankingOptions`, and filters. |\\\\n| `codeInterpreterTool(options?)` | Defaults to an auto-managed container when no `container` is provided. |\\\\n| `imageGenerationTool(options?)` | Supports image generation configuration such as `model`, `size`, `quality`, `background`, `inputFidelity`, `inputImageMask`, `moderation`, `outputCompression`, `partialImages`, and output format. |\\\\n| `toolSearchTool(options?)` | Adds the built-in `tool_search` helper. Pair it with deferred function tools or hosted MCP tools that set `deferLoading: true`. Supports hosted execution by default or client execution with `execution: 'client'` plus `execute`. |\\\\n| `programmaticToolCallingTool()` | Enables Programmatic Tool Calling. Pair it with tools whose `allowedCallers` includes `'programmatic'`. |\\\\n\\\\nThese helpers map JavaScript/TypeScript-friendly option names to the underlying OpenAI Responses API tool payloads. Refer to the official [OpenAI tools guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools) for the full tool schemas and advanced options like ranking options or semantic filters, the official [Tool search guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-tool-search) for the current built-in tool-search flow and model availability, and the official [Programmatic Tool Calling guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-programmatic-tool-calling) for model support and wire-level behavior.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Built-in execution tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “2. Built-in execution tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#2-built-in-execution-tools)\\\\n\\\\nThese tools are built into the SDK, but execution happens outside the model response itself:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Computer use** – implement the `Computer` interface and pass it to `computerTool()`. This always runs against a local `Computer` implementation that you provide.\\\\n*   **Shell** – either provide a local `Shell` implementation, or configure a hosted container environment with `shellTool({ environment })`.\\\\n*   **Apply patch** – implement the `Editor` interface and pass it to `applyPatchTool()`. This always runs against a local `Editor` implementation that you provide.\\\\n*   **Sandbox shell and filesystem tools** – use `shell()`, `filesystem()`, `skills()`, `memory()`, or `compaction()` on a `SandboxAgent` when those actions should run inside a sandbox workspace.\\\\n\\\\nThe tool calls are still requested by the model, but your application or configured execution environment performs the work.\\\\n\\\\nSandbox capability tools are different from process-wide built-in tools: they are bound to the live sandbox session for the current `SandboxAgent` run. Use [Sandbox agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sandbox-agents) when the tool should operate on the agent’s isolated workspace instead of your application process.\\\\n\\\\nBuilt-in execution tools\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  applyPatchTool,  computerTool,  shellTool,  Computer,  Editor,  Shell,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst computer: Computer = {  environment: 'browser',  dimensions: [1024, 768],  screenshot: async () => '',  click: async () => {},  doubleClick: async () => {},  scroll: async () => {},  type: async () => {},  wait: async () => {},  move: async () => {},  keypress: async () => {},  drag: async () => {},};\\\\nconst shell: Shell = {  run: async () => ({    output: [      {        stdout: '',        stderr: '',        outcome: { type: 'exit', exitCode: 0 },      },    ],  }),};\\\\nconst editor: Editor = {  createFile: async () => ({ status: 'completed' }),  updateFile: async () => ({ status: 'completed' }),  deleteFile: async () => ({ status: 'completed' }),};\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Local tools agent',  model: 'gpt-5.4',  tools: [    computerTool({ computer }),    shellTool({ shell, needsApproval: true }),    applyPatchTool({ editor, needsApproval: true }),  ],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Computer tool specifics\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Computer tool specifics”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#computer-tool-specifics)\\\\n\\\\n`computerTool()` accepts either:\\\\n\\\\n*   A concrete `Computer` instance.\\\\n*   An initializer function that creates a `Computer` per run.\\\\n*   A provider object with `{ create, dispose }` when you need run-scoped setup and teardown.\\\\n\\\\nTo use OpenAI’s current computer-use path, set a computer-capable model such as [`gpt-5.4`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4). When the request model is explicit, the SDK sends the GA built-in `computer` tool shape. If the effective model still comes from a stored prompt or another older integration, the SDK keeps the legacy `computer_use_preview` wire shape for compatibility unless you explicitly opt into the GA path with `modelSettings.toolChoice: 'computer'`.\\\\n\\\\nGA computer calls can contain batched `actions[]` in a single `computer_call`. The SDK executes them in order, evaluates `needsApproval` against each action, and returns the final screenshot as the tool output. If you build an approval UI from `interruption.rawItem`, read `actions` when present and fall back to `action` for legacy preview items.\\\\n\\\\nUse `needsApproval` when high-impact computer actions should pause for user review, and `onSafetyCheck` when you want to acknowledge or reject the pending safety checks reported for a computer call. For model-side guidance and migration details, see the official [OpenAI computer use guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-computer-use/) and its [migration note](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-computer-use/#migration-from-computer-use-preview).\\\\n\\\\n#### Shell tool specifics\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Shell tool specifics”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#shell-tool-specifics)\\\\n\\\\n`shellTool()` has two modes:\\\\n\\\\n*   Local mode: provide `shell`, and optionally `environment: { type: 'local', skills }` plus `needsApproval` and `onApproval` for automatic approval handling.\\\\n*   Hosted container mode: provide `environment` with `type: 'container_auto'` or `type: 'container_reference'`.\\\\n\\\\nIn local mode, `environment.skills` lets you mount local skills by `name`, `description`, and filesystem `path`.\\\\n\\\\nIn hosted container mode, configure `shellTool({ environment })` with either:\\\\n\\\\n*   `type: 'container_auto'` to create a managed container for the run.\\\\n*   `type: 'container_reference'` to reuse an existing container by `containerId`.\\\\n\\\\nHosted `container_auto` environments support:\\\\n\\\\n*   `networkPolicy`, including allowlists with `domainSecrets`.\\\\n*   `fileIds` for mounting uploaded files.\\\\n*   `memoryLimit` for container sizing.\\\\n*   `skills`, either by `skill_reference` or inline zip bundles.\\\\n\\\\nHosted shell environments do not accept `shell`, `needsApproval`, or `onApproval`, because the execution happens in the hosted container environment instead of your local process.\\\\n\\\\nSee `examples/tools/local-shell.ts`, `examples/tools/container-shell-skill-ref.ts`, and `examples/tools/container-shell-inline-skill.ts` for end-to-end usage.\\\\n\\\\n#### Apply-patch tool specifics\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Apply-patch tool specifics”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#apply-patch-tool-specifics)\\\\n\\\\n`applyPatchTool()` mirrors the local approval flow from `shellTool()`: use `needsApproval` to pause before file edits and `onApproval` when you want an app-level callback to auto-approve or reject.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Function tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “3. Function tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#3-function-tools)\\\\n\\\\nYou can turn **any** function into a tool with the `tool()` helper.\\\\n\\\\nFunction tool with Zod parameters\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { tool } from '@openai/agents';import { z } from 'zod';\\\\nconst getWeatherTool = tool({  name: 'get_weather',  description: 'Get the weather for a given city',  parameters: z.object({ city: z.string() }),  async execute({ city }) {    return `The weather in ${city} is sunny.`;  },});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Options reference\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Options reference”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#options-reference)\\\\n\\\\n| Field | Required | Description |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `name` | No | Defaults to the function name (e.g., `get_weather`). |\\\\n| `description` | Yes | Clear, human-readable description shown to the LLM. |\\\\n| `parameters` | Yes | A Zod schema, supported Standard Schema value, or raw JSON Schema object. Validation schemas automatically enable **strict** mode. |\\\\n| `strict` | No | When `true` (default), the SDK returns a model error if the arguments don’t validate. Set to `false` for fuzzy matching. |\\\\n| `execute` | Yes | `(args, context, details) => string | unknown | Promise<...>` – your business logic. Non-string outputs are serialized for the model. `context` is optional `RunContext`; `details` includes metadata like `toolCall`, `resumeState`, and `signal`. |\\\\n| `allowedCallers` | No | Responses-only non-empty list controlling whether the tool can be called directly, programmatically, or both. Use `'direct'`, `'programmatic'`, or both values. |\\\\n| `outputSchema` | No | Responses-only schema for the tool result. A Zod schema constrains the `execute` return type and validates/transforms the runtime result; a raw JSON schema describes the wire contract only. |\\\\n| `errorFunction` | No | Custom handler `(context, error, details) => result` for transforming internal errors into a model-visible result. When `outputSchema` is set, the result must satisfy that schema. The default handler is disabled so the original error is rethrown. |\\\\n| `timeoutMs` | No | Per-call timeout in milliseconds. Must be greater than 0 and less than or equal to `2147483647`. |\\\\n| `timeoutBehavior` | No | Timeout mode: `error_as_result` returns a model-visible result, and `raise_exception` throws `ToolTimeoutError`. The default is `error_as_result` without `outputSchema` and `raise_exception` with it. |\\\\n| `timeoutErrorFunction` | No | Custom handler `(context, timeoutError, details) => result` for `error_as_result`. When `outputSchema` is set, this handler is required and its result must satisfy the schema. |\\\\n| `customDataExtractor` | No | Callback `(context) => Record<string, unknown> | null | undefined` for attaching SDK-only metadata to the emitted `RunToolCallOutputItem.customData`. This data is not sent back to the model. |\\\\n| `needsApproval` | No | Require human approval before execution. See the [human-in-the-loop guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/human-in-the-loop). |\\\\n| `isEnabled` | No | Conditionally expose the tool per run; accepts a boolean or predicate. |\\\\n| `inputGuardrails` | No | Guardrails that run before the tool executes; can reject or throw. See [Guardrails](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/guardrails#tool-guardrails). |\\\\n| `outputGuardrails` | No | Guardrails that run after the tool executes; can reject or throw. See [Guardrails](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/guardrails#tool-guardrails). |\\\\n\\\\nSupported Standard Schema parameters are converted to JSON Schema for the model and validated locally before `execute` runs. The validation output type, including library transforms and defaults, becomes the inferred `execute` argument type. See [Schema validation](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/schemas) for a Valibot example and current limitations.\\\\n\\\\n#### SDK-only custom data\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “SDK-only custom data”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#sdk-only-custom-data)\\\\n\\\\nUse `customDataExtractor` when your application needs renderer hints, internal IDs, or other JSON-compatible metadata next to a tool result. The callback receives the run context, tool definition, model tool call, parsed input, output, and a cloned raw output item. Returned data is stored on `RunToolCallOutputItem.customData` and in `RunState`, but it is excluded from `history` and model replay.\\\\n\\\\n#### Function tool timeouts\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Function tool timeouts”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#function-tool-timeouts)\\\\n\\\\nUse `timeoutMs` to bound each function tool invocation.\\\\n\\\\n*   `timeoutBehavior: 'error_as_result'` returns `Tool '<name>' timed out after <timeoutMs>ms.` to the model. This is the default when `outputSchema` is not set.\\\\n*   `timeoutBehavior: 'raise_exception'` throws [`ToolTimeoutError`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents-core/classes/tooltimeouterror), which you can catch as part of [run exceptions](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents#exceptions).\\\\n*   `timeoutErrorFunction` lets you customize timeout text in `error_as_result` mode.\\\\n*   When `outputSchema` is set, the default changes to `raise_exception`. Using `error_as_result` requires a `timeoutErrorFunction` that returns a schema-compatible value.\\\\n*   Timeouts abort `details.signal`, so long-running tools can stop promptly when they listen for cancellation.\\\\n\\\\nIf you invoke a function tool directly, use [`invokeFunctionTool`](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/openai/agents/functions/invokefunctiontool) to enforce the same timeout behavior as normal agent runs.\\\\n\\\\n#### Non‑strict JSON‑schema tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Non‑strict JSON‑schema tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#nonstrict-jsonschema-tools)\\\\n\\\\nIf you need the model to _guess_ invalid or partial input you can disable strict mode when using raw JSON schema:\\\\n\\\\nNon-strict JSON schema tools\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { tool } from '@openai/agents';\\\\ninterface LooseToolInput {  text: string;}\\\\nconst looseTool = tool({  description: 'Echo input; be forgiving about typos',  strict: false,  parameters: {    type: 'object',    properties: { text: { type: 'string' } },    required: ['text'],    additionalProperties: true,  },  execute: async (input) => {    // because strict is false we need to do our own verification    if (typeof input !== 'object' || input === null || !('text' in input)) {      return 'Invalid input. Please try again';    }    return (input as LooseToolInput).text;  },});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n#### Deferred tool loading with tool search\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Deferred tool loading with tool search”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#deferred-tool-loading-with-tool-search)\\\\n\\\\nTool search lets the model load only the tool definitions it needs at runtime instead of sending every schema up front. In the SDK, this is how you work with deferred top-level function tools, `toolNamespace()` groups, and hosted MCP tools configured with `deferLoading: true`.\\\\n\\\\nUse Tool search only with GPT-5.4 and newer model releases that support it in the Responses API.\\\\n\\\\nDeferred tool loading with tool search\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, tool, toolNamespace, toolSearchTool } from '@openai/agents';import { z } from 'zod';\\\\nconst customerIdParams = z.object({  customerId: z.string().describe('The customer identifier to look up.'),});\\\\n// Keep a standalone deferred tool at the top level when it represents a// single searchable capability that does not need a shared namespace.const shippingLookup = tool({  name: 'get_shipping_eta',  description: 'Look up a shipment ETA by customer identifier.',  parameters: customerIdParams,  deferLoading: true,  async execute({ customerId }) {    return {      customerId,      eta: '2026-03-07',      carrier: 'Priority Express',    };  },});\\\\n// Group related tools into a namespace when one domain description should// cover several deferred tools and let tool search load them together.const crmTools = toolNamespace({  name: 'crm',  description: 'CRM tools for customer profile lookups.',  tools: [    tool({      name: 'get_customer_profile',      description: 'Fetch a basic customer profile.',      parameters: customerIdParams,      deferLoading: true,      async execute({ customerId }) {        return {          customerId,          tier: 'enterprise',        };      },    }),  ],});\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Operations assistant',  model: 'gpt-5.4',  // Mixing namespaced and top-level deferred tools in one request is supported.  tools: [shippingLookup, ...crmTools, toolSearchTool()],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe example intentionally mixes both styles:\\\\n\\\\n*   `shippingLookup` stays top-level because it is one standalone searchable capability.\\\\n*   `crmTools` uses `toolNamespace()` because related CRM tools share one high-level label and description.\\\\n*   Mixing namespaced and top-level deferred tools in the same request is supported; tool search can load both namespace paths such as `crm` and top-level paths such as `get_shipping_eta`.\\\\n\\\\nWhen you use tool search:\\\\n\\\\n*   Mark each deferred function tool with `deferLoading: true`.\\\\n*   Use `toolNamespace({ name, description, tools })` when multiple related tools should share one domain description and be loaded as a group.\\\\n*   Keep a tool top-level when it is a single independent capability and the tool name itself is a good search target.\\\\n*   Add `toolSearchTool()` to the same `tools` array whenever any deferred function tool or hosted MCP tool uses `deferLoading: true`.\\\\n*   Leave `modelSettings.toolChoice` on `'auto'`. The SDK rejects forcing the built-in `tool_search` tool or a deferred function tool by name.\\\\n*   Hosted execution is the default. If you set `toolSearchTool({ execution: 'client', execute })`, the standard `run()` loop only supports the built-in `{ paths: string[] }` client query shape; custom client-side schemas require your own Responses loop.\\\\n*   A namespace can mix immediate and deferred members. Immediate members stay callable without tool search, while deferred members in the same namespace are loaded on demand.\\\\n*   Deferred function tools and `toolNamespace()` are Responses-only. Chat Completions rejects them, and the AI SDK adapter does not support deferred Responses tool-loading flows.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Agents as tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “4. Agents as tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#4-agents-as-tools)\\\\n\\\\nSometimes you want an Agent to _assist_ another Agent without fully handing off the conversation. Use `agent.asTool()`:\\\\n\\\\nIf you are still choosing between `agent.asTool()` and `handoff()`, compare the patterns in the [Agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents#composition-patterns) and [Agent orchestration](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent).\\\\n\\\\nAgents as tools\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst summarizer = new Agent({  name: 'Summarizer',  instructions: 'Generate a concise summary of the supplied text.',});\\\\nconst summarizerTool = summarizer.asTool({  toolName: 'summarize_text',  toolDescription: 'Generate a concise summary of the supplied text.',});\\\\nconst mainAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Research assistant',  tools: [summarizerTool],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nUnder the hood the SDK:\\\\n\\\\n*   Creates a function tool with a single `input` parameter.\\\\n*   Runs the sub‑agent with that input when the tool is called.\\\\n*   Returns either the last message or the output extracted by `customOutputExtractor`.\\\\n\\\\nWhen an agent runs as a tool, the Agents SDK creates a `Runner` and uses that runner to execute the agent within the function-tool call. Pass `runConfig` to configure the nested runner and `runOptions` to configure the nested run.\\\\n\\\\nYou can also set `needsApproval` and `isEnabled` on the agent tool via `asTool()` options to integrate with human‑in‑the‑loop flows and conditional tool availability.\\\\n\\\\nInside `customOutputExtractor`, use `result.agentToolInvocation` to inspect the current `Agent.asTool()` invocation. In that callback the result always comes from `Agent.asTool()`, so `agentToolInvocation` is always defined and exposes `toolName`, `toolCallId`, and `toolArguments`. Use `result.runContext.context` for the application context. With the default single-`input` schema, `result.runContext.toolInput` is undefined; use `result.agentToolInvocation.toolArguments` to read the invocation arguments instead. When you configure custom `parameters` or an `inputBuilder`, `result.runContext.toolInput` contains the captured structured arguments. The `agentToolInvocation` metadata is scoped to the current nested invocation and is not serialized into `RunState`.\\\\n\\\\nRead agent tool invocation metadata\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst billingAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Billing Agent',  instructions: 'Handle billing questions and subscription changes.',});\\\\nconst billingTool = billingAgent.asTool({  toolName: 'billing_agent',  toolDescription: 'Handles customer billing questions.',  customOutputExtractor(result) {    console.log('tool', result.agentToolInvocation.toolName);    // Direct invoke() calls may not have a model-generated tool call id.    console.log('call', result.agentToolInvocation.toolCallId);    console.log('args', result.agentToolInvocation.toolArguments);\\\\n    return String(result.finalOutput ?? '');  },});\\\\nconst orchestrator = new Agent({  name: 'Support Orchestrator',  instructions: 'Delegate billing questions to the billing agent tool.',  tools: [billingTool],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nAdvanced structured-input options for `agent.asTool()`:\\\\n\\\\n*   `parameters`: replaces the default `{ input: string }` shape with a Zod schema, supported Standard Schema value, or raw JSON Schema.\\\\n*   `inputBuilder`: maps structured tool args to the nested agent input payload.\\\\n*   `includeInputSchema`: includes the input JSON schema in the nested run for stronger schema-aware behavior.\\\\n*   `resumeState`: controls context reconciliation strategy when resuming nested serialized `RunState`: `'merge'` (default) merges live approval/context state into the serialized state, `'replace'` uses the current run context instead, and `'preferSerialized'` resumes with the serialized context unchanged.\\\\n\\\\n#### Streaming events from agent tools\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Streaming events from agent tools”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#streaming-events-from-agent-tools)\\\\n\\\\nAgent tools can stream all nested run events back to your app. Choose the hook style that fits how you construct the tool:\\\\n\\\\nStreaming agent tools\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst billingAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Billing Agent',  instructions: 'Answer billing questions and compute simple charges.',});\\\\nconst billingTool = billingAgent.asTool({  toolName: 'billing_agent',  toolDescription: 'Handles customer billing questions.',  // onStream: simplest catch-all when you define the tool inline.  onStream: (event) => {    console.log(`[onStream] ${event.event.type}`, event);  },});\\\\n// on(eventName) lets you subscribe selectively (or use '*' for all).billingTool.on('run_item_stream_event', (event) => {  console.log('[on run_item_stream_event]', event);});billingTool.on('raw_model_stream_event', (event) => {  console.log('[on raw_model_stream_event]', event);});\\\\nconst orchestrator = new Agent({  name: 'Support Orchestrator',  instructions: 'Delegate billing questions to the billing agent tool.',  tools: [billingTool],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n*   Event types match `RunStreamEvent['type']`: `raw_model_stream_event`, `run_item_stream_event`, `agent_updated_stream_event`.\\\\n*   `onStream` is the simplest “catch-all” and works well when you declare the tool inline (`tools: [agent.asTool({ onStream })]`). Use it if you do not need per-event routing.\\\\n*   `on(eventName, handler)` lets you subscribe selectively (or with `'*'`) and is best when you need finer-grained handling or want to attach listeners after creation.\\\\n*   If you provide either `onStream` or any `on(...)` handler, the agent-as-tool will run in streaming mode automatically; without them it stays on the non-streaming path.\\\\n*   Handlers are invoked in parallel so a slow `onStream` callback will not block `on(...)` handlers (and vice versa).\\\\n*   `toolCallId` is provided when the tool was invoked via a model tool call; direct `invoke()` calls or provider quirks may omit it.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### 5. MCP servers\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “5. MCP servers”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#5-mcp-servers)\\\\n\\\\nYou can expose tools via [Model Context Protocol (MCP)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) servers and attach them to an agent. For instance, you can use `MCPServerStdio` to spawn and connect to the stdio MCP server:\\\\n\\\\nLocal MCP server\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, MCPServerStdio } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst server = new MCPServerStdio({  fullCommand: 'pnpm exec mcp-server-filesystem ./sample_files',});\\\\nawait server.connect();\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Assistant',  mcpServers: [server],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nSee [`filesystem-example.ts`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js/tree/main/examples/mcp/filesystem-example.ts) for a complete example. Also, if you’re looking for a comprehensive guide for MCP server tool integration, refer to [MCP guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/mcp) for details. When managing multiple servers (or partial failures), use `connectMcpServers` and the lifecycle guidance in the [MCP guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/mcp#managing-mcp-server-lifecycle).\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### 6. Experimental: Codex tool\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “6. Experimental: Codex tool”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#6-experimental-codex-tool)\\\\n\\\\n`@openai/agents-extensions/experimental/codex` provides `codexTool()`, a function tool that routes model tool calls to the Codex SDK so the agent can run workspace-scoped tasks (shell, file edits, MCP tools) autonomously. This surface is experimental and may change.\\\\n\\\\nInstall dependencies first:\\\\n\\\\nTerminal window\\\\n\\\\n`npm install @openai/agents-extensions @openai/codex-sdk`\\\\n\\\\nQuick start:\\\\n\\\\nExperimental Codex tool\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent } from '@openai/agents';import { codexTool } from '@openai/agents-extensions/experimental/codex';\\\\nexport const codexAgent = new Agent({  name: 'Codex Agent',  instructions:    'Use the codex tool to inspect the workspace and answer the question. When skill names, which usually start with `$`, are mentioned, you must rely on the codex tool to use the skill and answer the question.',  tools: [    codexTool({      sandboxMode: 'workspace-write',      workingDirectory: '/path/to/repo',      defaultThreadOptions: {        model: 'gpt-5.4',        networkAccessEnabled: true,        webSearchEnabled: false,      },    }),  ],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWhat to know:\\\\n\\\\n*   Auth: supply `CODEX_API_KEY` (preferred) or `OPENAI_API_KEY`, or pass `codexOptions.apiKey`.\\\\n*   Inputs: strict schema—`inputs` must contain at least one `{ type: 'text', text }` or `{ type: 'local_image', path }`.\\\\n*   Safety: pair `sandboxMode` with `workingDirectory`; set `skipGitRepoCheck` if the directory is not a Git repo.\\\\n*   Threading: `useRunContextThreadId: true` reads/stores the latest thread id in `runContext.context`, which is useful for cross-turn reuse in your app state.\\\\n*   Thread ID precedence: tool call `threadId` (if your schema includes it) takes priority, then run-context thread id, then `codexTool({ threadId })`.\\\\n*   Run context key: defaults to `codexThreadId` for `name: 'codex'`, or `codexThreadId_<suffix>` for names like `name: 'engineer'` (`codex_engineer` after normalization).\\\\n*   Mutable context requirement: when `useRunContextThreadId` is enabled, pass a mutable object or `Map` as `run(..., { context })`.\\\\n*   Naming: tool names are normalized into the `codex` namespace (`engineer` becomes `codex_engineer`), and duplicate Codex tool names in an agent are rejected.\\\\n*   Streaming: `onStream` mirrors Codex events (reasoning, command execution, MCP tool calls, file changes, web search) so you can log or trace progress.\\\\n*   Outputs: tool result includes `response`, `usage`, and `threadId`, and Codex token usage is recorded in `RunContext`.\\\\n*   Structure: `outputSchema` can be a descriptor, JSON schema object, or Zod object. For JSON object schemas, `additionalProperties` must be `false`.\\\\n\\\\nRun-context thread reuse example:\\\\n\\\\nCodex run-context thread reuse\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';import { codexTool } from '@openai/agents-extensions/experimental/codex';\\\\n// Derived from codexTool({ name: 'engineer' }) when runContextThreadIdKey is omitted.type ExampleContext = {  codexThreadId_engineer?: string;};\\\\nconst agent = new Agent<ExampleContext>({  name: 'Codex assistant',  instructions: 'Use the codex tool for workspace tasks.',  tools: [    codexTool({      // `name` is optional for a single Codex tool.      // We set it so the run-context key is tool-specific and to avoid collisions when adding more Codex tools.      name: 'engineer',      // Reuse the same Codex thread across runs that share this context object.      useRunContextThreadId: true,      sandboxMode: 'workspace-write',      workingDirectory: '/path/to/repo',      defaultThreadOptions: {        model: 'gpt-5.4',        approvalPolicy: 'never',      },    }),  ],});\\\\n// The default key for useRunContextThreadId with name=engineer is codexThreadId_engineer.const context: ExampleContext = {};\\\\n// First turn creates (or resumes) a Codex thread and stores the thread ID in context.await run(agent, 'Inspect src/tool.ts and summarize it.', { context });// Second turn reuses the same thread because it shares the same context object.await run(agent, 'Now list refactoring opportunities.', { context });\\\\nconst threadId = context.codexThreadId_engineer;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Programmatic Tool Calling\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Programmatic Tool Calling”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#programmatic-tool-calling)\\\\n\\\\nProgrammatic Tool Calling lets a supported Responses model generate JavaScript that coordinates several tool calls inside a hosted execution environment. Your application still executes client-owned tools, so existing validation, permissions, approvals, guardrails, and side effects continue to apply.\\\\n\\\\nProgrammatic Tool Calling\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, programmaticToolCallingTool, tool } from '@openai/agents';import { z } from 'zod';\\\\nconst getInventory = tool({  name: 'get_inventory',  description: 'Return inventory for a SKU.',  parameters: z.object({ sku: z.string() }),  allowedCallers: ['programmatic'],  outputSchema: z.object({    sku: z.string(),    availableUnits: z.number(),  }),  async execute({ sku }) {    return { sku, availableUnits: 42 };  },});\\\\nconst getDemand = tool({  name: 'get_demand',  description: 'Return requested units for a SKU.',  parameters: z.object({ sku: z.string() }),  allowedCallers: ['programmatic'],  outputSchema: z.object({    sku: z.string(),    requestedUnits: z.number(),  }),  async execute({ sku }) {    return { sku, requestedUnits: 31 };  },});\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Inventory planner',  model: 'gpt-5.6',  instructions: `Use Programmatic Tool Calling to fetch inventory and demand concurrently.Return the source values and the calculated shortage in the final answer.  `.trim(),  tools: [getInventory, getDemand, programmaticToolCallingTool()],});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nSetup has two parts:\\\\n\\\\n1.   Add `programmaticToolCallingTool()` to the agent.\\\\n2.   Set `allowedCallers` on each tool that the generated program may call.\\\\n\\\\n| `allowedCallers` | Behavior |\\\\n| --- | --- |\\\\n| Omitted or `['direct']` | The model can call the tool directly. |\\\\n| `['programmatic']` | Only the generated program can call the tool. |\\\\n| `['direct', 'programmatic']` | Either the model or the generated program can call the tool. |\\\\n\\\\nThe SDK supports programmatic callers for tools created with `tool()`, local or hosted `shellTool()`, `applyPatchTool()`, `hostedMcpTool()`, and `codeInterpreterTool()`.\\\\n\\\\nThe SDK validates the configuration before sending a request. A programmatic-only tool requires `programmaticToolCallingTool()`. The helper also requires at least one eligible tool unless the request includes tool search or a stored prompt that can provide one.\\\\n\\\\nUse `outputSchema` when a function tool must return structured data. A Zod schema constrains the `execute` return type and validates and transforms the runtime result. A raw JSON schema describes the wire contract but does not add SDK-side result validation. An invalid Zod result raises `InvalidToolOutputError`.\\\\n\\\\nStructured outputs also change failure handling:\\\\n\\\\n*   The default `errorFunction` is disabled, so execution errors are rethrown. A custom handler must return a value compatible with `outputSchema`.\\\\n*   The default timeout behavior becomes `'raise_exception'`.\\\\n*   To use `'error_as_result'`, provide a `timeoutErrorFunction` whose return value satisfies `outputSchema`.\\\\n*   A value substituted by an output guardrail must also satisfy `outputSchema`.\\\\n\\\\nProgrammatic Tool Calling is Responses-only. Chat Completions, Realtime agents, and the AI SDK model adapter reject these options. When an eligible tool is deferred, tool search must load it before a later generated program can call it.\\\\n\\\\nSee [`examples/tools/programmatic-tool-calling.ts`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js/tree/main/examples/tools/programmatic-tool-calling.ts) for a complete example.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n##
