agents\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Agent Orchestration\\\\n\\\\nOrchestration refers to the flow of agents in your app. Which agents run, in what order, and how do they decide what happens next? There are two main ways to orchestrate agents:\\\\n\\\\n> Read this page after the [Quickstart](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart) or the [Agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents#composition-patterns). This page is about workflow design across multiple agents, not the `Agent` constructor itself.\\\\n\\\\n1.   Allowing the LLM to make decisions: this uses the intelligence of an LLM to plan, reason, and decide on what steps to take based on that.\\\\n2.   Orchestrating via code: determining the flow of agents via your code.\\\\n\\\\nYou can mix and match these patterns. Each has their own tradeoffs, described below.\\\\n\\\\n## Orchestrating via LLM\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Orchestrating via LLM”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#orchestrating-via-llm)\\\\n\\\\nAn agent is an LLM equipped with instructions, tools and handoffs. This means that given an open-ended task, the LLM can autonomously plan how it will tackle the task, using tools to take actions and acquire data, and using handoffs to delegate tasks to sub-agents. For example, a research agent could be equipped with tools like:\\\\n\\\\n*   Web search to find information online\\\\n*   File search and retrieval to search through proprietary data and connections\\\\n*   Computer use to take actions on a computer\\\\n*   Code execution to do data analysis\\\\n*   Handoffs to specialized agents that are great at planning, report writing and more.\\\\n\\\\n### Core SDK patterns\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Core SDK patterns”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#core-sdk-patterns)\\\\n\\\\nIn the Agents SDK, two orchestration patterns come up most often:\\\\n\\\\n| Pattern | How it works | Best when |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| Agents as tools | A manager agent keeps control of the conversation and calls specialist agents through `agent.asTool()`. | You want one agent to own the final answer, combine outputs from multiple specialists, or enforce shared guardrails in one place. |\\\\n| Handoffs | A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist, and that specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. | You want the specialist to speak directly to the user, keep prompts focused, or use different instructions/models per specialist. |\\\\n\\\\nUse **agents as tools** when the specialist should help with a subtask but should not take over the user-facing conversation. The manager stays responsible for deciding which tools to call and how to present the final response. See the [tools guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#4-agents-as-tools) for the API details, and the [agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents#composition-patterns) for a side-by-side example.\\\\n\\\\nUse **handoffs** when routing itself is part of the workflow and you want the selected specialist to own the next part of the conversation. The handoff preserves the conversation context while narrowing the active instructions to the specialist. See the [handoffs guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/handoffs) for the API, and the [quickstart](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#define-your-handoffs) for the smallest end-to-end example.\\\\n\\\\nYou can combine the two patterns. A triage agent might hand off to a specialist, and that specialist can still use other agents as tools for bounded subtasks.\\\\n\\\\nThis pattern is great when the task is open-ended and you want to rely on the intelligence of an LLM. The most important tactics here are:\\\\n\\\\n1.   Invest in good prompts. Make it clear what tools are available, how to use them, and what parameters it must operate within.\\\\n2.   Monitor your app and iterate on it. See where things go wrong, and iterate on your prompts.\\\\n3.   Allow the agent to introspect and improve. For example, run it in a loop, and let it critique itself; or, provide error messages and let it improve.\\\\n4.   Have specialized agents that excel in one task, rather than having a general purpose agent that is expected to be good at anything.\\\\n5.   Invest in [evals](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals). This lets you train your agents to improve and get better at tasks.\\\\n\\\\nIf you want the SDK primitives behind this style of orchestration, start with [tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools), [handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/handoffs), and [running agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents).\\\\n\\\\n## Orchestrating via code\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Orchestrating via code”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#orchestrating-via-code)\\\\n\\\\nWhile orchestrating via LLM is powerful, orchestrating via code makes tasks more deterministic and predictable, in terms of speed, cost and performance. Common patterns here are:\\\\n\\\\n*   Using [structured outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) to generate well formed data that you can inspect with your code. For example, you might ask an agent to classify the task into a few categories, and then pick the next agent based on the category.\\\\n*   Chaining multiple agents by transforming the output of one into the input of the next. You can decompose a task like writing a blog post into a series of steps - do research, write an outline, write the blog post, critique it, and then improve it.\\\\n*   Running the agent that performs the task in a `while` loop with an agent that evaluates and provides feedback, until the evaluator says the output passes certain criteria.\\\\n*   Running multiple agents in parallel, e.g. via JavaScript primitives like `Promise.all`. This is useful for speed when you have multiple tasks that don’t depend on each other.\\\\n\\\\nWe have a number of examples in [`examples/agent-patterns`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js/tree/main/examples/agent-patterns).\\\\n\\\\n## Related guides\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Related guides”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#related-guides)\\\\n\\\\n*   [Agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents) for composition patterns and agent configuration.\\\\n*   [Tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#4-agents-as-tools) for `agent.asTool()` and manager-style orchestration.\\\\n*   [Handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/handoffs) for delegation between specialist agents.\\\\n*   [Running Agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents) for `Runner` and per-run orchestration controls.\\\\n* agents\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Agent Orchestration\\\\n\\\\nOrchestration refers to the flow of agents in your app. Which agents run, in what order, and how do they decide what happens next? There are two main ways to orchestrate agents:\\\\n\\\\n> Read this page after the [Quickstart](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart) or the [Agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents#composition-patterns). This page is about workflow design across multiple agents, not the `Agent` constructor itself.\\\\n\\\\n1.   Allowing the LLM to make decisions: this uses the intelligence of an LLM to plan, reason, and decide on what steps to take based on that.\\\\n2.   Orchestrating via code: determining the flow of agents via your code.\\\\n\\\\nYou can mix and match these patterns. Each has their own tradeoffs, described below.\\\\n\\\\n## Orchestrating via LLM\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Orchestrating via LLM”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#orchestrating-via-llm)\\\\n\\\\nAn agent is an LLM equipped with instructions, tools and handoffs. This means that given an open-ended task, the LLM can autonomously plan how it will tackle the task, using tools to take actions and acquire data, and using handoffs to delegate tasks to sub-agents. For example, a research agent could be equipped with tools like:\\\\n\\\\n*   Web search to find information online\\\\n*   File search and retrieval to search through proprietary data and connections\\\\n*   Computer use to take actions on a computer\\\\n*   Code execution to do data analysis\\\\n*   Handoffs to specialized agents that are great at planning, report writing and more.\\\\n\\\\n### Core SDK patterns\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Core SDK patterns”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#core-sdk-patterns)\\\\n\\\\nIn the Agents SDK, two orchestration patterns come up most often:\\\\n\\\\n| Pattern | How it works | Best when |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| Agents as tools | A manager agent keeps control of the conversation and calls specialist agents through `agent.asTool()`. | You want one agent to own the final answer, combine outputs from multiple specialists, or enforce shared guardrails in one place. |\\\\n| Handoffs | A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist, and that specialist becomes the active agent for the rest of the turn. | You want the specialist to speak directly to the user, keep prompts focused, or use different instructions/models per specialist. |\\\\n\\\\nUse **agents as tools** when the specialist should help with a subtask but should not take over the user-facing conversation. The manager stays responsible for deciding which tools to call and how to present the final response. See the [tools guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools#4-agents-as-tools) for the API details, and the [agents guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/agents#composition-patterns) for a side-by-side example.\\\\n\\\\nUse **handoffs** when routing itself is part of the workflow and you want the selected specialist to own the next part of the conversation. The handoff preserves the conversation context while narrowing the active instructions to the specialist. See the [handoffs guide](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/handoffs) for the API, and the [quickstart](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/quickstart#define-your-handoffs) for the smallest end-to-end example.\\\\n\\\\nYou can combine the two patterns. A triage agent might hand off to a specialist, and that specialist can still use other agents as tools for bounded subtasks.\\\\n\\\\nThis pattern is great when the task is open-ended and you want to rely on the intelligence of an LLM. The most important tactics here are:\\\\n\\\\n1.   Invest in good prompts. Make it clear what tools are available, how to use them, and what parameters it must operate within.\\\\n2.   Monitor your app and iterate on it. See where things go wrong, and iterate on your prompts.\\\\n3.   Allow the agent to introspect and improve. For example, run it in a loop, and let it critique itself; or, provide error messages and let it improve.\\\\n4.   Have specialized agents that excel in one task, rather than having a general purpose agent that is expected to be good at anything.\\\\n5.   Invest in [evals](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/evals). This lets you train your agents to improve and get better at tasks.\\\\n\\\\nIf you want the SDK primitives behind this style of orchestration, start with [tools](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/tools), [handoffs](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/handoffs), and [running agents](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/running-agents).\\\\n\\\\n## Orchestrating via code\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Orchestrating via code”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/multi-agent#orchestrating-via-code)\\\\n\\\\nWhile orchestrating via LLM is powerful, orchestrating via code makes tasks more deterministic and predictable, in terms of speed, cost and performance. Common patterns here are:\\\\n\\\\n*   Using [structured outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) to generate well formed data that you can inspect with your code. For example, you might ask an agent to classify the task into a few categories, and then pick the next agent based on the category.\\\\n*   Chaining multiple agents by transforming the output of one into the input of the next. You can decompose a task like writing a blog post into a series of steps - do research, write an outline, write the blog post, critique it, and then improve it.\\\\n*   Running the agent that performs the task in a `while` loop with an agent that evaluates and provides feedback, until the evaluator says the output passes certain criteria.\\\\n*   Running multiple agents in parallel, e.g. via JavaScript primitives like `Promise.all`. This is useful for speed when you have multiple tasks that don’t depend on each other.\\\\n\\\\nWe have a number of examples in [`examples/agent-patterns`](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-js/tree/main/examples/agent-patterns).\\\\n\\\\n## Related guides\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Related runs.\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Sessions\\\\n\\\\nSessions give the Agents SDK a **persistent memory layer**. Provide any object that implements the `Session` interface to `Runner.run`, and the SDK handles the rest. When a session is present, the runner automatically:\\\\n\\\\n1.   Fetches previously stored conversation items and prepends them to the next turn.\\\\n2.   Persists new user input and assistant output after each run completes.\\\\n3.   Keeps the session available for future turns, whether you call the runner with new user text or resume from an interrupted `RunState`.\\\\n\\\\nThis removes the need to manually call `toInputList()` or stitch history between turns. The TypeScript SDK ships with two implementations: `OpenAIConversationsSession` for the Conversations API and `MemorySession`, which is intended for local development. Because they share the `Session` interface, you can plug in your own storage backend. For inspiration beyond the Conversations API, explore the sample session backends under `examples/memory/` (Prisma, file-backed, and more). When you use an OpenAI Responses model, wrap any session with `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` to automatically shrink stored conversation history via [`responses.compact`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/responses/compact).\\\\n\\\\n> Tip: To run the `OpenAIConversationsSession` examples on this page, set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable (or provide an `apiKey` when constructing the session) so the SDK can call the Conversations API.\\\\n\\\\nUse sessions when you want the SDK to manage client-side memory for you. If you are already using OpenAI server-managed state with `conversationId` or `previousResponseId`, you usually do not also need a session for the same conversation history.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Getting started\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Getting started”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#getting-started)\\\\n\\\\n### Quick start\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Quick start”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#quick-start)\\\\n\\\\nUse `OpenAIConversationsSession` to sync memory with the [Conversations API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/conversations), or swap in any other `Session` implementation.\\\\n\\\\nUse the Conversations API as session memory\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, OpenAIConversationsSession, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'TourGuide',  instructions: 'Answer with compact travel facts.',});\\\\n// Any object that implements the Session interface works here. This example uses// the built-in OpenAIConversationsSession, but you can swap in a custom Session.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession();\\\\nconst firstTurn = await run(agent, 'What city is the Golden Gate Bridge in?', {  session,});console.log(firstTurn.finalOutput); // \\\\\\\"San Francisco\\\\\\\"\\\\nconst secondTurn = await run(agent, 'What state is it in?', { session });console.log(secondTurn.finalOutput); // \\\\\\\"California\\\\\\\"\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nReusing the same session instance ensures the agent receives the full conversation history before every turn and automatically persists new items. Switching to a different `Session` implementation requires no other code changes.\\\\n\\\\nFor local demos, tests, or process-local chat state, `MemorySession` provides the same interface without talking to OpenAI:\\\\n\\\\nUse MemorySession for local state\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, MemorySession, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'TourGuide',  instructions: 'Answer with compact travel facts.',});\\\\nconst session = new MemorySession();const result = await run(agent, 'What city is the Golden Gate Bridge in?', {  session,});\\\\nconsole.log(result.finalOutput);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIConversationsSession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `conversationId` | `string` | Reuse an existing conversation instead of creating one lazily. |\\\\n| `client` | `OpenAI` | Pass a preconfigured OpenAI client. |\\\\n| `apiKey` | `string` | API key used when creating an internal OpenAI client. |\\\\n| `baseURL` | `string` | Base URL for OpenAI-compatible endpoints. |\\\\n| `organization` | `string` | OpenAI organization ID for requests. |\\\\n| `project` | `string` | OpenAI project ID for requests. |\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `sessionId` | `string` | Stable identifier for logs or tests. Generated automatically by default. |\\\\n| `initialItems` | `AgentInputItem[]` | Seed the session with existing history. |\\\\n| `logger` | `Logger` | Override the logger used for debug output. |\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` stores everything in local process memory, so it is reset when your process exits.\\\\n\\\\nIf you need to pre-create a conversation ID before constructing the session, use `startOpenAIConversationsSession(client?)` and pass the returned ID as `conversationId`.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Core session behavior\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Core session behavior”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#core-session-behavior)\\\\n\\\\n### How the runner uses sessions\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “How the runner uses sessions”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#how-the-runner-uses-sessions)\\\\n\\\\n*   **Before each run** it retrieves the session history, merges it with the new turn’s input, and passes the combined list to your agent.\\\\n*   **After a non-streaming run** one call to `session.addItems()` persists both the original user input and the model outputs from the latest turn.\\\\n*   **For streaming runs** it writes the user input first and appends streamed outputs once the turn completes.\\\\n*   **When resuming from `RunResult.state`** (for approvals or other interruptions) keep passing the same `session`. The resumed turn is added to memory without re-preparing the input.\\\\n\\\\nWhen an output guardrail rejects a terminal function-tool result, the runner does not add the raw rejected result to new session history. The runner persists a replay-safe placeholder for a recognized function call and result pair, and omits an ambiguous current-response suffix rather than storing output whose ownership it cannot prove. This protection does not undo external tool side effects or erase data that an application stored outside the session pipeline.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### Inspecting and editing history\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Inspecting and editing history”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#inspecting-and-editing-history)\\\\n\\\\nSessions expose simple CRUD helpers so you can build “undo”, “clear chat”, or audit features.\\\\n\\\\nRead and edit stored items\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { OpenAIConversationsSession } from '@openai/agents';import type { AgentInputItem } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\n// Replace OpenAIConversationsSession with any other Session implementation that// supports get/add/pop/clear if you store history elsewhere.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession({  conversationId: 'conv_123', // Resume an existing conversation if you have one.});\\\\nconst history = await session.getItems();console.log(`Loaded ${history.length} prior items.`);\\\\nconst followUp: AgentInputItem[] = [  {    type: 'message',    role: 'user',    content: [{ type: 'input_text', text: 'Let’s continue later.' }],  },];await session.addItems(followUp);\\\\nconst undone = await session.popItem();\\\\nif (undone?.type === 'message') {  console.log(undone.role); // \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\"}\\\\nawait session.clearSession();\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`session.getItems()` returns the stored `AgentInputItem[]`. Call `popItem()` to remove the last entry—useful for user corrections before you rerun the agent.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Custom storage and merge behavior\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Custom storage and merge behavior”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#custom-storage-and-merge-behavior)\\\\n\\\\n### Bring your own storage\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Bring your own storage”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#bring-your-own-storage)\\\\n\\\\nImplement the `Session` interface to back memory with Redis, DynamoDB, SQLite, or another datastore. Only five asynchronous methods are required.\\\\n\\\\nCustom in-memory session implementation\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';import { randomUUID } from '@openai/agents-core/_shims';import { getLogger } from '@openai/agents-core';import type { AgentInputItem, Session } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\n/** * Minimal example of a Session implementation; swap this class for any storage-backed version. */export class CustomMemorySession implements Session {  private readonly sessionId: string;  private readonly logger: ReturnType<typeof getLogger>;\\\\n  private items: AgentInputItem[];\\\\n  constructor(    options: {      sessionId?: string;      initialItems?: AgentInputItem[];      logger?: ReturnType<typeof getLogger>;    } = {},  ) {    this.sessionId = options.sessionId ?? randomUUID();    this.items = options.initialItems      ? options.initialItems.map(cloneAgentItem)      : [];    this.logger = options.logger ?? getLogger('openai-agents:memory-session');  }\\\\n  async getSessionId(): Promise<string> {    return this.sessionId;  }\\\\n  async getItems(limit?: number): Promise<AgentInputItem[]> {    if (limit === undefined) {      const cloned = this.items.map(cloneAgentItem);      this.logger.debug(        `Getting items from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,      );      return cloned;    }    if (limit <= 0) {      return [];    }    const start = Math.max(this.items.length - limit, 0);    const items = this.items.slice(start).map(cloneAgentItem);    this.logger.debug(      `Getting items from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(items)}`,    );    return items;  }\\\\n  async addItems(items: AgentInputItem[]): Promise<void> {    if (items.length === 0) {      return;    }    const cloned = items.map(cloneAgentItem);    this.logger.debug(      `Adding items to memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,    );    this.items = [...this.items, ...cloned];  }\\\\n  async popItem(): Promise<AgentInputItem | undefined> {    if (this.items.length === 0) {      return undefined;    }    const item = this.items[this.items.length - 1];    const cloned = cloneAgentItem(item);    this.logger.debug(      `Popping item from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,    );    this.items = this.items.slice(0, -1);    return cloned;  }\\\\n  async clearSession(): Promise<void> {    this.logger.debug(`Clearing memory session (${this.sessionId})`);    this.items = [];  }}\\\\nfunction cloneAgentItem<T extends AgentInputItem>(item: T): T {  return structuredClone(item);}\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'MemoryDemo',  instructions: 'Remember the running total.',});\\\\n// Using the above custom memory session implementation hereconst session = new CustomMemorySession({  sessionId: 'session-123-4567',});\\\\nconst first = await run(agent, 'Add 3 to the total.', { session });console.log(first.finalOutput);\\\\nconst second = await run(agent, 'Add 4 more.', { session });console.log(second.finalOutput);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nCustom sessions let you enforce retention policies, add encryption, or attach metadata to each conversation turn before persisting it.\\\\n\\\\n### Make custom persistence atomic and idempotent\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Make custom persistence atomic and idempotent”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#make-custom-persistence-atomic-and-idempotent)\\\\n\\\\nFor backends that can update history and record an operation identifier atomically, implement the optional `SessionHistoryTransactionAwareSession` interface. Its `applyHistoryTransaction(...)` method receives a stable `operationId` and one of two transaction shapes:\\\\n\\\\n*   `append_items` appends a group of history items.\\\\n*   `replace_suffix` replaces an expected history suffix only when the currently stored suffix still matches.\\\\n\\\\nPersist the operation identifier and history mutation in the same backend transaction. Repeating an operation identifier with the same transaction must succeed without applying it twice. Reusing the identifier with different content, or applying `replace_suffix` after its expected suffix changed, must fail without changing history. This lets the runner safely reconcile persisted output across retries and resumable output-guardrail flows.\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` implements this contract as a reference. Existing `Session` implementations remain valid without it, but they do not opt into transaction-aware persistence paths.\\\\n\\\\n### Scope custom sessions with the run context\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Scope custom sessions with the run context”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#scope-custom-sessions-with-the-run-context)\\\\n\\\\nImplement `RunContextAwareSession<TContext>` and set `acceptsRunContext` to `true` when a custom session needs the active `RunContext` for storage routing or metadata. The runner passes the same context instance to all history operations during a run, including streamed persistence and resumed runs. Sessions that only implement `Session` keep the existing method signatures and are called without the additional argument.\\\\n\\\\nPartition session history with the run context\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  run,  type AgentInputItem,  type RunContext,  type RunContextAwareSession,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\ntype TenantContext = {  tenantId: string;};\\\\nclass TenantSession implements RunContextAwareSession<TenantContext> {  readonly acceptsRunContext = true;  private readonly itemsByTenant = new Map<string, AgentInputItem[]>();\\\\n  async getSessionId(): Promise<string> {    return 'shared-tenant-session';  }\\\\n  async getItems(    limit?: number,    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<AgentInputItem[]> {    const items = this.getTenantItems(runContext);    return limit === undefined ? [...items] : items.slice(-limit);  }\\\\n  async addItems(    items: AgentInputItem[],    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<void> {    this.getTenantItems(runContext).push(...items);  }\\\\n  async popItem(    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<AgentInputItem | undefined> {    return this.getTenantItems(runContext).pop();  }\\\\n  async clearSession(runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>): Promise<void> {    this.itemsByTenant.set(this.getTenantId(runContext), []);  }\\\\n  private getTenantItems(    runContext: RunContext<TenantContext> | undefined,  ): AgentInputItem[] {    const tenantId = this.getTenantId(runContext);    const items = this.itemsByTenant.get(tenantId) ?? [];    this.itemsByTenant.set(tenantId, items);    return items;  }\\\\n  private getTenantId(    runContext: RunContext<TenantContext> | undefined,  ): string {    if (!runContext) {      throw new Error('TenantSession requires a run context.');    }    return runContext.context.tenantId;  }}\\\\nconst agent = new Agent<TenantContext>({  name: 'Assistant',  instructions: 'Reply concisely.',});const session = new TenantSession();\\\\nawait run(agent, 'Remember that my favorite color is green.', {  context: { tenantId: 'tenant-a' },  session,});\\\\nawait run(agent, 'What is my favorite color?', {  context: { tenantId: 'tenant-a' },  session,});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` does not forward a run context to its underlying session. Keep one compaction-session instance per context scope if you combine these capabilities.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### Control how history and new items merge\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Control how history and new items merge”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#control-how-history-and-new-items-merge)\\\\n\\\\nWhen you pass an array of `AgentInputItem`s as the run input, provide a `sessionInputCallback` to merge them with stored history deterministically. The runner loads the existing history, calls your callback **before the model invocation**, and hands the returned array to the model as the turn’s complete input. This hook is ideal for trimming old items, deduplicating tool results, or highlighting only the context you want the model to see.\\\\n\\\\nTruncate history with sessionInputCallback\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, OpenAIConversationsSession, run } from '@openai/agents';import type { AgentInputItem } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Planner',  instructions: 'Track outstanding tasks before responding.',});\\\\n// Any Session implementation can be passed here; customize storage as needed.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession();\\\\nconst todoUpdate: AgentInputItem[] = [  {    type: 'message',    role: 'user',    content: [      { type: 'input_text', text: 'Add booking a hotel to my todo list.' },    ],  },];\\\\nawait run(agent, todoUpdate, {  session,  // function that combines session history with new input items before the model call  sessionInputCallback: (history, newItems) => {    const recentHistory = history.slice(-8);    return [...recentHistory, ...newItems];  },});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor string inputs the runner merges history automatically, so the callback is optional. The callback only runs when your turn input is already an item array.\\\\n\\\\nIf you are also using `conversationId` or `previousResponseId`, keep at least one new item from the current turn in the callback result. Those server-managed APIs depend on the current-turn delta. If the callback drops every new item, the SDK restores the original new inputs and logs a warning instead of sending an empty delta.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Resumable runs\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Resumable runs”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#resumable-runs)\\\\n\\\\n### Handling approvals and resumable runs\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Handling approvals and resumable runs”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#handling-approvals-and-resumable-runs)\\\\n\\\\nHuman-in-the-loop flows often pause a run to wait for approval:\\\\n\\\\nResume a run with the same session\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, MemorySession, Runner } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Trip Planner',  instructions: 'Plan trips and ask for approval before booking anything.',});\\\\nconst runner = new Runner();const session = new MemorySession();\\\\nconst result = await runner.run(agent, 'Search the itinerary', {  session,});\\\\nif (result.interruptions?.length) {  // ... collect user feedback, then resume the agent in a later turn.  for (const interruption of result.interruptions) {    result.state.approve(interruption);  }\\\\n  const continuation = await runner.run(agent, result.state, { session });  console.log(continuation.finalOutput);}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWhen you resume from a previous `RunState`, the new turn is appended to the same memory record to preserve a single conversation history. Most human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval checkpoints round-trip through `RunState` while the session keeps the conversation history complete.\\\\n\\\\nOutput guardrails impose a stricter boundary when an approved function-tool result can become the final output. If a serialized checkpoint does not contain enough provenance to identify the current output safely, the SDK fails closed before further model, tool, or session side effects. Some output-bearing approval checkpoints therefore cannot be resumed from serialized state with a session attached. Start a new run from safe input when the SDK reports this condition; do not work around it by replaying the rejected raw items.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Advanced: history compaction\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Advanced: history compaction”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#advanced-history-compaction)\\\\n\\\\n### Compact OpenAI Responses history automatically\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Compact OpenAI Responses history automatically”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#compact-openai-responses-history-automatically)\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` decorates any `Session` and uses the OpenAI Responses API to replace a long stored history with a shorter equivalent list of conversation items. After each persisted turn the runner passes the latest `responseId` into `runCompaction`, which calls `responses.compact` when your decision hook returns true. Depending on `compactionMode`, the request is built either from the latest Responses API chain or from the session’s current items. The default trigger compacts once at least 10 non-user items have accumulated; override `shouldTriggerCompaction` to base the decision on token counts or custom heuristics. After compaction returns, the decorator clears the underlying session and rewrites it with the reduced item list, so avoid pairing it with `OpenAIConversationsSession`, which uses a different server-managed history flow.\\\\n\\\\nDecorate a session with OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  MemorySession,  OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession,  run,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Support',  instructions: 'Answer briefly and keep track of prior context.',  model: 'gpt-5.4',});\\\\n// Wrap any Session to trigger responses.compact once history grows beyond your threshold.const session = new OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession({  // You can pass any Session implementation except OpenAIConversationsSession  underlyingSession: new MemorySession(),  // (optional) The model used for calling responses.compact API  model: 'gpt-5.4',  // (optional) your custom logic here  shouldTriggerCompaction: ({ compactionCandidateItems }) => {    return compactionCandidateItems.length >= 12;  },});\\\\nawait run(agent, 'Summarize order #8472 in one sentence.', { session });await run(agent, 'Remind me of the shipping address.', { session });\\\\n// Compaction runs automatically after each persisted turn. You can also force it manually.await session.runCompaction({ force: true });\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `client` | `OpenAI` | OpenAI client used for `responses.compact`. |\\\\n| `underlyingSession` | `Session` | Backing session store to clear/rewrite with compacted items. Defaults to an in-memory session for demos and must not be `OpenAIConversationsSession`. |\\\\n| `model` | `OpenAI.ResponsesModel` | Model used for compaction requests. Defaults to the SDK’s current default OpenAI model. |\\\\n| `compactionMode` | `'auto' | 'previous_response_id' | 'input'` | Controls whether compaction uses server response chaining or local input items. |\\\\n| `shouldTriggerCompaction` | `(context) => boolean | Promise<boolean>` | Custom trigger hook based on `responseId`, `compactionMode`, candidate items, and current session items. |\\\\n\\\\n`compactionMode: 'previous_response_id'` is useful when you are already chaining turns with Responses API response IDs. `compactionMode: 'input'` rebuilds compaction requests from the current session items instead, which is helpful when the response chain is unavailable or you want the underlying session contents to be the source of truth.\\\\n\\\\n`runCompaction(args)` options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `responseId` | `string` | Latest Responses API response id for `previous_response_id` mode. |\\\\n| `compactionMode` | `'auto' | 'previous_response_id' | 'input'` | Optional per-call override of the configured mode. |\\\\n| `store` | `boolean` | Indicates whether the last run stored server state. |\\\\n| `force` | `boolean` | Bypass `shouldTriggerCompaction` and compact immediately. |\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` serializes mutations issued through the same wrapper instance. Calls to `runCompaction()`, `addItems()`, `popItem()`, and `clearSession()` run in invocation order, and the queue continues after a rejected operation, so later wrapper mutations do not interleave with replacement or rollback. A successful replacement or rollback keeps the wrapper’s cached history aligned with the underlying session. If both replacement and restoration fail, recover the underlying session before continuing. This ordering guarantee does not coordinate a different wrapper instance or direct mutation of `underlyingSession`; coordinate those access paths in your application.\\\\n\\\\n#### Manual compaction for low-latency streaming\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Manual compaction for low-latency streaming”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#manual-compaction-for-low-latency-streaming)\\\\n\\\\nCompaction clears and rewrites the underlying session, so the SDK waits for it before resolving a streaming run. If compaction is heavy, `result.completed` can stay pending for a few seconds after the last output token. For low-latency streaming or faster turn-taking, disable auto-compaction and call `runCompaction` yourself between turns (or during idle time).\\\\n\\\\nDisable auto-compaction and compact between turns\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  MemorySession,  OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession,  run,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Support',  instructions: 'Answer briefly and keep track of prior context.',  model: 'gpt-5.4',});\\\\n// Disable auto-compaction to avoid delaying stream completion.const session = new OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession({  underlyingSession: new MemorySession(),  shouldTriggerCompaction: () => false,});\\\\nconst result = await run(agent, 'Share the latest ticket update.', {  session,  stream: true,});\\\\n// Wait for the streaming run to finish before compacting.await result.completed;\\\\n// Choose force based on your own thresholds or heuristics, between turns or during idle time.await session.runCompaction({ force: true });\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nYou can call `runCompaction({ force: true })` at any time to shrink history before archiving or handoff. runs.\\\",\\\"url\\\":\\\"https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Sessions\\\\n\\\\nSessions give the Agents SDK a **persistent memory layer**. Provide any object that implements the `Session` interface to `Runner.run`, and the SDK handles the rest. When a session is present, the runner automatically:\\\\n\\\\n1.   Fetches previously stored conversation items and prepends them to the next turn.\\\\n2.   Persists new user input and assistant output after each run completes.\\\\n3.   Keeps the session available for future turns, whether you call the runner with new user text or resume from an interrupted `RunState`.\\\\n\\\\nThis removes the need to manually call `toInputList()` or stitch history between turns. The TypeScript SDK ships with two implementations: `OpenAIConversationsSession` for the Conversations API and `MemorySession`, which is intended for local development. Because they share the `Session` interface, you can plug in your own storage backend. For inspiration beyond the Conversations API, explore the sample session backends under `examples/memory/` (Prisma, file-backed, and more). When you use an OpenAI Responses model, wrap any session with `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` to automatically shrink stored conversation history via [`responses.compact`](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/responses/compact).\\\\n\\\\n> Tip: To run the `OpenAIConversationsSession` examples on this page, set the `OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable (or provide an `apiKey` when constructing the session) so the SDK can call the Conversations API.\\\\n\\\\nUse sessions when you want the SDK to manage client-side memory for you. If you are already using OpenAI server-managed state with `conversationId` or `previousResponseId`, you usually do not also need a session for the same conversation history.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Getting started\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Getting started”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#getting-started)\\\\n\\\\n### Quick start\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Quick start”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#quick-start)\\\\n\\\\nUse `OpenAIConversationsSession` to sync memory with the [Conversations API](https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/conversations), or swap in any other `Session` implementation.\\\\n\\\\nUse the Conversations API as session memory\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, OpenAIConversationsSession, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'TourGuide',  instructions: 'Answer with compact travel facts.',});\\\\n// Any object that implements the Session interface works here. This example uses// the built-in OpenAIConversationsSession, but you can swap in a custom Session.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession();\\\\nconst firstTurn = await run(agent, 'What city is the Golden Gate Bridge in?', {  session,});console.log(firstTurn.finalOutput); // \\\\\\\"San Francisco\\\\\\\"\\\\nconst secondTurn = await run(agent, 'What state is it in?', { session });console.log(secondTurn.finalOutput); // \\\\\\\"California\\\\\\\"\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nReusing the same session instance ensures the agent receives the full conversation history before every turn and automatically persists new items. Switching to a different `Session` implementation requires no other code changes.\\\\n\\\\nFor local demos, tests, or process-local chat state, `MemorySession` provides the same interface without talking to OpenAI:\\\\n\\\\nUse MemorySession for local state\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, MemorySession, run } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'TourGuide',  instructions: 'Answer with compact travel facts.',});\\\\nconst session = new MemorySession();const result = await run(agent, 'What city is the Golden Gate Bridge in?', {  session,});\\\\nconsole.log(result.finalOutput);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIConversationsSession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `conversationId` | `string` | Reuse an existing conversation instead of creating one lazily. |\\\\n| `client` | `OpenAI` | Pass a preconfigured OpenAI client. |\\\\n| `apiKey` | `string` | API key used when creating an internal OpenAI client. |\\\\n| `baseURL` | `string` | Base URL for OpenAI-compatible endpoints. |\\\\n| `organization` | `string` | OpenAI organization ID for requests. |\\\\n| `project` | `string` | OpenAI project ID for requests. |\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `sessionId` | `string` | Stable identifier for logs or tests. Generated automatically by default. |\\\\n| `initialItems` | `AgentInputItem[]` | Seed the session with existing history. |\\\\n| `logger` | `Logger` | Override the logger used for debug output. |\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` stores everything in local process memory, so it is reset when your process exits.\\\\n\\\\nIf you need to pre-create a conversation ID before constructing the session, use `startOpenAIConversationsSession(client?)` and pass the returned ID as `conversationId`.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Core session behavior\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Core session behavior”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#core-session-behavior)\\\\n\\\\n### How the runner uses sessions\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “How the runner uses sessions”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#how-the-runner-uses-sessions)\\\\n\\\\n*   **Before each run** it retrieves the session history, merges it with the new turn’s input, and passes the combined list to your agent.\\\\n*   **After a non-streaming run** one call to `session.addItems()` persists both the original user input and the model outputs from the latest turn.\\\\n*   **For streaming runs** it writes the user input first and appends streamed outputs once the turn completes.\\\\n*   **When resuming from `RunResult.state`** (for approvals or other interruptions) keep passing the same `session`. The resumed turn is added to memory without re-preparing the input.\\\\n\\\\nWhen an output guardrail rejects a terminal function-tool result, the runner does not add the raw rejected result to new session history. The runner persists a replay-safe placeholder for a recognized function call and result pair, and omits an ambiguous current-response suffix rather than storing output whose ownership it cannot prove. This protection does not undo external tool side effects or erase data that an application stored outside the session pipeline.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### Inspecting and editing history\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Inspecting and editing history”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#inspecting-and-editing-history)\\\\n\\\\nSessions expose simple CRUD helpers so you can build “undo”, “clear chat”, or audit features.\\\\n\\\\nRead and edit stored items\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { OpenAIConversationsSession } from '@openai/agents';import type { AgentInputItem } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\n// Replace OpenAIConversationsSession with any other Session implementation that// supports get/add/pop/clear if you store history elsewhere.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession({  conversationId: 'conv_123', // Resume an existing conversation if you have one.});\\\\nconst history = await session.getItems();console.log(`Loaded ${history.length} prior items.`);\\\\nconst followUp: AgentInputItem[] = [  {    type: 'message',    role: 'user',    content: [{ type: 'input_text', text: 'Let’s continue later.' }],  },];await session.addItems(followUp);\\\\nconst undone = await session.popItem();\\\\nif (undone?.type === 'message') {  console.log(undone.role); // \\\\\\\"user\\\\\\\"}\\\\nawait session.clearSession();\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`session.getItems()` returns the stored `AgentInputItem[]`. Call `popItem()` to remove the last entry—useful for user corrections before you rerun the agent.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Custom storage and merge behavior\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Custom storage and merge behavior”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#custom-storage-and-merge-behavior)\\\\n\\\\n### Bring your own storage\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Bring your own storage”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#bring-your-own-storage)\\\\n\\\\nImplement the `Session` interface to back memory with Redis, DynamoDB, SQLite, or another datastore. Only five asynchronous methods are required.\\\\n\\\\nCustom in-memory session implementation\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, run } from '@openai/agents';import { randomUUID } from '@openai/agents-core/_shims';import { getLogger } from '@openai/agents-core';import type { AgentInputItem, Session } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\n/** * Minimal example of a Session implementation; swap this class for any storage-backed version. */export class CustomMemorySession implements Session {  private readonly sessionId: string;  private readonly logger: ReturnType<typeof getLogger>;\\\\n  private items: AgentInputItem[];\\\\n  constructor(    options: {      sessionId?: string;      initialItems?: AgentInputItem[];      logger?: ReturnType<typeof getLogger>;    } = {},  ) {    this.sessionId = options.sessionId ?? randomUUID();    this.items = options.initialItems      ? options.initialItems.map(cloneAgentItem)      : [];    this.logger = options.logger ?? getLogger('openai-agents:memory-session');  }\\\\n  async getSessionId(): Promise<string> {    return this.sessionId;  }\\\\n  async getItems(limit?: number): Promise<AgentInputItem[]> {    if (limit === undefined) {      const cloned = this.items.map(cloneAgentItem);      this.logger.debug(        `Getting items from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,      );      return cloned;    }    if (limit <= 0) {      return [];    }    const start = Math.max(this.items.length - limit, 0);    const items = this.items.slice(start).map(cloneAgentItem);    this.logger.debug(      `Getting items from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(items)}`,    );    return items;  }\\\\n  async addItems(items: AgentInputItem[]): Promise<void> {    if (items.length === 0) {      return;    }    const cloned = items.map(cloneAgentItem);    this.logger.debug(      `Adding items to memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,    );    this.items = [...this.items, ...cloned];  }\\\\n  async popItem(): Promise<AgentInputItem | undefined> {    if (this.items.length === 0) {      return undefined;    }    const item = this.items[this.items.length - 1];    const cloned = cloneAgentItem(item);    this.logger.debug(      `Popping item from memory session (${this.sessionId}): ${JSON.stringify(cloned)}`,    );    this.items = this.items.slice(0, -1);    return cloned;  }\\\\n  async clearSession(): Promise<void> {    this.logger.debug(`Clearing memory session (${this.sessionId})`);    this.items = [];  }}\\\\nfunction cloneAgentItem<T extends AgentInputItem>(item: T): T {  return structuredClone(item);}\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'MemoryDemo',  instructions: 'Remember the running total.',});\\\\n// Using the above custom memory session implementation hereconst session = new CustomMemorySession({  sessionId: 'session-123-4567',});\\\\nconst first = await run(agent, 'Add 3 to the total.', { session });console.log(first.finalOutput);\\\\nconst second = await run(agent, 'Add 4 more.', { session });console.log(second.finalOutput);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nCustom sessions let you enforce retention policies, add encryption, or attach metadata to each conversation turn before persisting it.\\\\n\\\\n### Make custom persistence atomic and idempotent\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Make custom persistence atomic and idempotent”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#make-custom-persistence-atomic-and-idempotent)\\\\n\\\\nFor backends that can update history and record an operation identifier atomically, implement the optional `SessionHistoryTransactionAwareSession` interface. Its `applyHistoryTransaction(...)` method receives a stable `operationId` and one of two transaction shapes:\\\\n\\\\n*   `append_items` appends a group of history items.\\\\n*   `replace_suffix` replaces an expected history suffix only when the currently stored suffix still matches.\\\\n\\\\nPersist the operation identifier and history mutation in the same backend transaction. Repeating an operation identifier with the same transaction must succeed without applying it twice. Reusing the identifier with different content, or applying `replace_suffix` after its expected suffix changed, must fail without changing history. This lets the runner safely reconcile persisted output across retries and resumable output-guardrail flows.\\\\n\\\\n`MemorySession` implements this contract as a reference. Existing `Session` implementations remain valid without it, but they do not opt into transaction-aware persistence paths.\\\\n\\\\n### Scope custom sessions with the run context\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Scope custom sessions with the run context”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#scope-custom-sessions-with-the-run-context)\\\\n\\\\nImplement `RunContextAwareSession<TContext>` and set `acceptsRunContext` to `true` when a custom session needs the active `RunContext` for storage routing or metadata. The runner passes the same context instance to all history operations during a run, including streamed persistence and resumed runs. Sessions that only implement `Session` keep the existing method signatures and are called without the additional argument.\\\\n\\\\nPartition session history with the run context\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  run,  type AgentInputItem,  type RunContext,  type RunContextAwareSession,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\ntype TenantContext = {  tenantId: string;};\\\\nclass TenantSession implements RunContextAwareSession<TenantContext> {  readonly acceptsRunContext = true;  private readonly itemsByTenant = new Map<string, AgentInputItem[]>();\\\\n  async getSessionId(): Promise<string> {    return 'shared-tenant-session';  }\\\\n  async getItems(    limit?: number,    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<AgentInputItem[]> {    const items = this.getTenantItems(runContext);    return limit === undefined ? [...items] : items.slice(-limit);  }\\\\n  async addItems(    items: AgentInputItem[],    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<void> {    this.getTenantItems(runContext).push(...items);  }\\\\n  async popItem(    runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>,  ): Promise<AgentInputItem | undefined> {    return this.getTenantItems(runContext).pop();  }\\\\n  async clearSession(runContext?: RunContext<TenantContext>): Promise<void> {    this.itemsByTenant.set(this.getTenantId(runContext), []);  }\\\\n  private getTenantItems(    runContext: RunContext<TenantContext> | undefined,  ): AgentInputItem[] {    const tenantId = this.getTenantId(runContext);    const items = this.itemsByTenant.get(tenantId) ?? [];    this.itemsByTenant.set(tenantId, items);    return items;  }\\\\n  private getTenantId(    runContext: RunContext<TenantContext> | undefined,  ): string {    if (!runContext) {      throw new Error('TenantSession requires a run context.');    }    return runContext.context.tenantId;  }}\\\\nconst agent = new Agent<TenantContext>({  name: 'Assistant',  instructions: 'Reply concisely.',});const session = new TenantSession();\\\\nawait run(agent, 'Remember that my favorite color is green.', {  context: { tenantId: 'tenant-a' },  session,});\\\\nawait run(agent, 'What is my favorite color?', {  context: { tenantId: 'tenant-a' },  session,});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` does not forward a run context to its underlying session. Keep one compaction-session instance per context scope if you combine these capabilities.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n### Control how history and new items merge\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Control how history and new items merge”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#control-how-history-and-new-items-merge)\\\\n\\\\nWhen you pass an array of `AgentInputItem`s as the run input, provide a `sessionInputCallback` to merge them with stored history deterministically. The runner loads the existing history, calls your callback **before the model invocation**, and hands the returned array to the model as the turn’s complete input. This hook is ideal for trimming old items, deduplicating tool results, or highlighting only the context you want the model to see.\\\\n\\\\nTruncate history with sessionInputCallback\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, OpenAIConversationsSession, run } from '@openai/agents';import type { AgentInputItem } from '@openai/agents-core';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Planner',  instructions: 'Track outstanding tasks before responding.',});\\\\n// Any Session implementation can be passed here; customize storage as needed.const session = new OpenAIConversationsSession();\\\\nconst todoUpdate: AgentInputItem[] = [  {    type: 'message',    role: 'user',    content: [      { type: 'input_text', text: 'Add booking a hotel to my todo list.' },    ],  },];\\\\nawait run(agent, todoUpdate, {  session,  // function that combines session history with new input items before the model call  sessionInputCallback: (history, newItems) => {    const recentHistory = history.slice(-8);    return [...recentHistory, ...newItems];  },});\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor string inputs the runner merges history automatically, so the callback is optional. The callback only runs when your turn input is already an item array.\\\\n\\\\nIf you are also using `conversationId` or `previousResponseId`, keep at least one new item from the current turn in the callback result. Those server-managed APIs depend on the current-turn delta. If the callback drops every new item, the SDK restores the original new inputs and logs a warning instead of sending an empty delta.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Resumable runs\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Resumable runs”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#resumable-runs)\\\\n\\\\n### Handling approvals and resumable runs\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Handling approvals and resumable runs”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#handling-approvals-and-resumable-runs)\\\\n\\\\nHuman-in-the-loop flows often pause a run to wait for approval:\\\\n\\\\nResume a run with the same session\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport { Agent, MemorySession, Runner } from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Trip Planner',  instructions: 'Plan trips and ask for approval before booking anything.',});\\\\nconst runner = new Runner();const session = new MemorySession();\\\\nconst result = await runner.run(agent, 'Search the itinerary', {  session,});\\\\nif (result.interruptions?.length) {  // ... collect user feedback, then resume the agent in a later turn.  for (const interruption of result.interruptions) {    result.state.approve(interruption);  }\\\\n  const continuation = await runner.run(agent, result.state, { session });  console.log(continuation.finalOutput);}\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWhen you resume from a previous `RunState`, the new turn is appended to the same memory record to preserve a single conversation history. Most human-in-the-loop (HITL) approval checkpoints round-trip through `RunState` while the session keeps the conversation history complete.\\\\n\\\\nOutput guardrails impose a stricter boundary when an approved function-tool result can become the final output. If a serialized checkpoint does not contain enough provenance to identify the current output safely, the SDK fails closed before further model, tool, or session side effects. Some output-bearing approval checkpoints therefore cannot be resumed from serialized state with a session attached. Start a new run from safe input when the SDK reports this condition; do not work around it by replaying the rejected raw items.\\\\n\\\\n* * *\\\\n\\\\n## Advanced: history compaction\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Advanced: history compaction”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#advanced-history-compaction)\\\\n\\\\n### Compact OpenAI Responses history automatically\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Compact OpenAI Responses history automatically”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#compact-openai-responses-history-automatically)\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` decorates any `Session` and uses the OpenAI Responses API to replace a long stored history with a shorter equivalent list of conversation items. After each persisted turn the runner passes the latest `responseId` into `runCompaction`, which calls `responses.compact` when your decision hook returns true. Depending on `compactionMode`, the request is built either from the latest Responses API chain or from the session’s current items. The default trigger compacts once at least 10 non-user items have accumulated; override `shouldTriggerCompaction` to base the decision on token counts or custom heuristics. After compaction returns, the decorator clears the underlying session and rewrites it with the reduced item list, so avoid pairing it with `OpenAIConversationsSession`, which uses a different server-managed history flow.\\\\n\\\\nDecorate a session with OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  MemorySession,  OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession,  run,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Support',  instructions: 'Answer briefly and keep track of prior context.',  model: 'gpt-5.4',});\\\\n// Wrap any Session to trigger responses.compact once history grows beyond your threshold.const session = new OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession({  // You can pass any Session implementation except OpenAIConversationsSession  underlyingSession: new MemorySession(),  // (optional) The model used for calling responses.compact API  model: 'gpt-5.4',  // (optional) your custom logic here  shouldTriggerCompaction: ({ compactionCandidateItems }) => {    return compactionCandidateItems.length >= 12;  },});\\\\nawait run(agent, 'Summarize order #8472 in one sentence.', { session });await run(agent, 'Remind me of the shipping address.', { session });\\\\n// Compaction runs automatically after each persisted turn. You can also force it manually.await session.runCompaction({ force: true });\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` constructor options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `client` | `OpenAI` | OpenAI client used for `responses.compact`. |\\\\n| `underlyingSession` | `Session` | Backing session store to clear/rewrite with compacted items. Defaults to an in-memory session for demos and must not be `OpenAIConversationsSession`. |\\\\n| `model` | `OpenAI.ResponsesModel` | Model used for compaction requests. Defaults to the SDK’s current default OpenAI model. |\\\\n| `compactionMode` | `'auto' | 'previous_response_id' | 'input'` | Controls whether compaction uses server response chaining or local input items. |\\\\n| `shouldTriggerCompaction` | `(context) => boolean | Promise<boolean>` | Custom trigger hook based on `responseId`, `compactionMode`, candidate items, and current session items. |\\\\n\\\\n`compactionMode: 'previous_response_id'` is useful when you are already chaining turns with Responses API response IDs. `compactionMode: 'input'` rebuilds compaction requests from the current session items instead, which is helpful when the response chain is unavailable or you want the underlying session contents to be the source of truth.\\\\n\\\\n`runCompaction(args)` options:\\\\n\\\\n| Option | Type | Notes |\\\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\\\n| `responseId` | `string` | Latest Responses API response id for `previous_response_id` mode. |\\\\n| `compactionMode` | `'auto' | 'previous_response_id' | 'input'` | Optional per-call override of the configured mode. |\\\\n| `store` | `boolean` | Indicates whether the last run stored server state. |\\\\n| `force` | `boolean` | Bypass `shouldTriggerCompaction` and compact immediately. |\\\\n\\\\n`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` serializes mutations issued through the same wrapper instance. Calls to `runCompaction()`, `addItems()`, `popItem()`, and `clearSession()` run in invocation order, and the queue continues after a rejected operation, so later wrapper mutations do not interleave with replacement or rollback. A successful replacement or rollback keeps the wrapper’s cached history aligned with the underlying session. If both replacement and restoration fail, recover the underlying session before continuing. This ordering guarantee does not coordinate a different wrapper instance or direct mutation of `underlyingSession`; coordinate those access paths in your application.\\\\n\\\\n#### Manual compaction for low-latency streaming\\\\n\\\\n[Section titled “Manual compaction for low-latency streaming”](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-js/guides/sessions#manual-compaction-for-low-latency-streaming)\\\\n\\\\nCompaction clears and rewrites the underlying session, so the SDK waits for it before resolving a streaming run. If compaction is heavy, `result.completed` can stay pending for a few seconds after the last output token. For low-latency streaming or faster turn-taking, disable auto-compaction and call `runCompaction` yourself between turns (or during idle time).\\\\n\\\\nDisable auto-compaction and compact between turns\\\\n\\\\n```\\\\nimport {  Agent,  MemorySession,  OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession,  run,} from '@openai/agents';\\\\nconst agent = new Agent({  name: 'Support',  instructions: 'Answer briefly and keep track of prior context.',  model: 'gpt-5.4',});\\\\n// Disable auto-compaction to avoid delaying stream completion.const session = new OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession({  underlyingSession: new MemorySession(),  shouldTriggerCompaction: () => false,});\\\\nconst result = await run(agent, 'Share the latest ticket update.', {  session,  stream: true,});\\\\n// Wait for the streaming run to finish before compacting.await result.completed;\\\\n// Choose force based on your own thresholds or heuristics, between turns or during idle time.await session.runCompaction({ force: true });\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nYou can call `runCompaction({ force: true })` at any time to shrink history before archiving or handoff.
